items.content_excerpt: $INTC $MU $NVDA $QQQ $SPY The Rookie Error: Bears incorrectly assume that if an AI model becomes "leaner and faster," enterprises will buy fewer memory chips. items.title: $AAPL A massive engineering & strategic move under Tim Cook. Apple fully transitioned its Mac lineup from Intel processors to its own cu
items.content_excerpt: $AAPL A massive engineering & strategic move under Tim Cook. Apple fully transitioned its Mac lineup from Intel processors to its own custom ARM-based chips (M1 & successors), completing the shift by 2023. It’s a huge Performance + efficiency leap. Macs got dramatically better battery life, speed, and thermals almost overnight—often outperforming higher-power Intel machines while staying cooler and quieter. The integration of CPU, GPU, Neural Engine, and unified memory let hardware and software work together far more tightly than before. Apple no longer depended on Intel’s roadmap (or delays). It could design chips specifically optimized for macOS, iOS apps running on Mac, and future features like on-device AI. It forced competitors to rethink laptop performance-per-watt and accelerated the broader shift toward custom silicon in PCs. Many reviewers and analysts still rank this as one of the defining technical achievements of the post-Jobs era. And something else about condom usage.

items.title: @Toorichtocare Agree on the funding point, and the filings back it up: fiscal 2026 operating cash flow was $182.9B against $115.9B spent on
items.content_excerpt: @Toorichtocare Agree on the funding point, and the filings back it up: fiscal 2026 operating cash flow was $182.9B against $115.9B spent on property and equipment, and long-term debt actually fell from $40.2B to $31.1B. The piece I'd keep an eye on is leases. Microsoft stretched data-center useful lives from 15 to 25 years starting this fiscal year, which pushes more future leases into operating leases that don't count as capex. That's partly why the calendar-2026 capex outlook dropped to about $175B from $190B with the plan itself unchanged. So the cash-funded story holds, but lease commitments are where hidden leverage would show up. Disclosure: I own $MSFT.

items.content_excerpt: @Techdamentals Worth flagging for anyone plugging $AMZN into a valuation model: Q2 net income of $62.6B included $53.4B of pre-tax non-operating income, mostly from the Anthropic investment, so trailing EPS overstates the run rate. The cash side is the opposite story. Operating cash flow was $161.4B over the last twelve months, up 33%, and the negative FCF comes entirely from $169.0B of net equipment spending. Whether that spending pays off probably comes down to how fast the $496B AWS backlog turns into revenue. Full disclosure, AMZN is one of my holdings.

items.title: $PLTZ $PLTR The competition is catching up: • The Standardization of the "Moat": Palantir’s primary historical advantage was doing
items.content_excerpt: $PLTZ $PLTR The competition is catching up: • The Standardization of the "Moat": Palantir’s primary historical advantage was doing the brutal, unglamorous engineering work of connecting siloed data systems. Today, open protocols like Model Context Protocol (MCP) and native headless API layers mean any developer can connect disparate software systems in days, rather than months. The "data plumbing" problem is being solved globally. • Hyperscaler Muscle: Microsoft, AWS, and Google are no longer just providing cloud storage. They are building robust enterprise agent frameworks, data fabric layers (like Microsoft Fabric), and security governance tools natively into the infrastructure companies already pay for. • The "Good Enough" Threshold: A co. might look at Palantir's price tag and say, "Why buy the whole operating system when we can use headless Salesforce APIs, an open-source vector database, and Anthropic's MCP to build a 'good enough' orchestration layer for a fraction of the cost?"

items.content_excerpt: $PLTZ AI discussion: It feels like $PLTR was always in a tub where there was only an inch of water for competition, but now it seems as if the water level is rising faster than Palantir is growing taller. That "rising water" analogy is a remarkably accurate way to describe the psychological shift happening in enterprise software right now. For years, Palantir operated in what felt like a private, ankle-deep pond—they were virtually the only company with a fully functional data ontology, defense-grade security, and a platform capable of orchestrating highly complex enterprise systems. They were "tall" enough to stand completely clear of standard software vendors. But now, the headless software movement, open-source frameworks, and hyperscaler AI stacks are acting like an open faucet, rapidly filling that tub. The gap between what Palantir does and what the rest of the tech ecosystem can do is narrowing.

items.title: $UAL spends heavily on jet fuel, its largest operating expense, drawn from the same distillate cut of crude that produces diesel and the fue
items.content_excerpt: $UAL spends heavily on jet fuel, its largest operating expense, drawn from the same distillate cut of crude that produces diesel and the fuel oil now showing up sharply in the inflation report. A refining shortage across three major regions tightened that cut of the barrel earlier this year. Fuel oil, which heats homes rather than planes, rose 52% from a year earlier in August as a result. Core inflation, at 2.4% in August, excludes energy costs like these specifically because they can swing violently and later reverse when refining capacity returns. Full explainer, plain English: https://youtu.be/le-mFDuzQd8 Educational, not advice. https://techdamentals.com/newsletter/why-cpi-and-core-inflation-tell-different-stories?ref=st

items.content_excerpt: $IOVA Simply moved lower with broader market weakness. $XBI itself was down 3.65%. All key moving averages are still rising, and the uptrend remains intact. I actually expect some profit-taking following positive catalyst news in late October or mid-November, particularly if the stock makes another explosive move toward $18–30 and becomes technically extended after such a strong run this year. With the next major catalysts potentially months away, a sell-the-news reaction wouldn't surprise me. If we get that kind of move, I'll watch price action and volume for signs of exhaustion or reversal and look to lock in some profits rather than blindly hold through a potential correction. Still very bullish on the long-term thesis for 2H FY2027

$PLTZ $PLTR The competition is catching up: • The Standardization of the "Moat": Palantir’s primary historical advantage was doing the brutal, unglamorous engineering work of connecting siloed data systems. Today, open protocols like Model Context Protocol (MCP) and native headless API layers mean any developer can connect disparate software systems in days, rather than months. The "data plumbing" problem is being solved globally. • Hyperscaler Muscle: Microsoft, AWS, and Google are no longer just providing cloud storage. They are building robust enterprise agent frameworks, data fabric layers (like Microsoft Fabric), and security governance tools natively into the infrastructure companies already pay for. • The "Good Enough" Threshold: A co. might look at Palantir's price tag and say, "Why buy the whole operating system when we can use headless Salesforce APIs, an open-source vector database, and Anthropic's MCP to build a 'good enough' orchestration layer for a fraction of the cost?"
